name: StratInvest Advisory Group
title: Learning to build the whole business.
deck: A company-formation startup became my education in connecting a website, a customer journey, and the operations behind them.
sections: A broader kind of responsibility

At StratInvest, I worked on a business helping people establish companies in the UAE. The service brought together company registration, residency-related requirements, and the practical questions that come with getting started in another country. My role grew across marketing, sales, the website, and operations.

After tutoring and an early corporate role, this was an opportunity to take responsibility for more of the picture. I worked closely with a mentor, learning how the different parts of a young business depended on each other. A clear message mattered, but so did what happened after someone responded to it.
Making the service understandable

I worked on the company’s identity, branding, website structure, and copy. The challenge was to make a complicated service easier to navigate: explain what the business offered, help prospective clients understand the next step, and connect that step to a workable registration process.

My LinkedIn experience also describes building the website with the help of AI tools. What I carry forward from that work is the need to understand the service before deciding how to present it. A page can look finished while the journey behind it still needs work.
The form was part of the product

The client application form became a central part of registration. I worked on conditional questions in Typeform, where one answer changed which questions appeared next. This required thinking through the logic of different client situations, rather than presenting everyone with the same long questionnaire.

That logic connected the website to the operational work. The information collected had to be useful to the people handling the request. For me, it was a practical lesson in user experience: clarity comes from knowing which question to ask, and when to ask it.
Taking the work into the market

I also handled client communications and sales work, including quotations and webinars introducing StratInvest. Those conversations gave the service another test: could I explain the offer clearly enough for someone to understand its relevance to them?

The marketing budget was limited in a competitive industry. I had to connect creative decisions with the reality of reaching customers. Building the website and registration journey was only part of the challenge; the business also needed a sustainable way to generate relevant demand.
What stayed with me

When the venture paused, my mentor helped me take the next step toward working in Dubai. The business chapter ended, but the skills did not disappear. Website thinking, onboarding logic, communication, and operational coordination became part of how I approached later work.

I now bring that wider view into education and business development. I am more interested in how all the parts work together, and more aware that the experience someone sees on the surface depends on many decisions underneath it.
takeaway: A useful website begins with understanding the business behind it.

name: AC & Associates
title: Clarity, inside and out.
deck: A freelance engagement connecting business development and operations with the way a business presents itself online.
sections: Where the work began

My work with AC & Associates brought together two areas I had been developing: the practical side of running a business and the way that business communicates. Between February and June 2024, I contributed through a freelance contract covering business-development advice, logistics, operational procedures, and website content.

The scope crossed the boundary between internal work and the customer-facing experience. That connection is what makes the project meaningful to me. How a business explains itself is closely tied to how well it understands and organizes what it does.
Looking at the operational side

I advised on business-development initiatives and supported work on logistics and more streamlined operational procedures. These were practical contributions to how work was organized and moved forward.

This extended the perspective I was building through StratInvest. Instead of looking at communication as an isolated task, I was learning to see it alongside the decisions, coordination, and processes that keep a business moving.
Content as part of the experience

On the website, I worked on strategic content structure and copywriting to support the user experience and the rebranding effort. The contribution went beyond choosing words: structure affects what a visitor encounters first, how ideas relate to one another, and how easily the business can be understood.

I see this as one of the useful overlaps between writing and business development. Writing forces you to decide what matters. Organizing that writing forces you to decide what someone else needs to understand before moving on.
A connection I kept building

AC & Associates is a small but important part of my journey toward work that combines communication with operational thinking. The photograph from my LinkedIn project is a reminder that this work also happens through conversations and working relationships.
The lesson I take from the engagement is to look in both directions: inward at how the business works, and outward at how someone experiences it. I want the two to support each other.
takeaway: How a business works and how it explains itself belong in the same conversation.
images: A working conversation with Ali F. Chahin, shared with the project on LinkedIn.

name: Studypedia
title: An opportunity becomes real when someone shows up.
deck: Student outreach, personal conversations, and the 2022 international educational fair that helped me understand the value of trust.
sections: Starting with a student network

By the time I worked with Studypedia, tutoring had already connected me with many students at LAU. People knew me through studying together, asking for help, and finding someone who could explain a difficult topic. That network opened a different kind of opportunity: helping students discover possibilities beyond Lebanon.

As a brand ambassador, I supported Studypedia’s awareness and outreach. The work centered on connecting people with opportunities to explore studying abroad, including options in Europe, the United States, and the United Kingdom.
Giving people a reason to attend

A major part of the role was promoting the second International Educational Fair in October 2022. The event took place at the Radisson Blu in Verdun. My contribution involved targeted outreach and personalized communication with prospective attendees.

The value of the event had to feel relevant to the person receiving the invitation. Academic plans, professional ambitions, and uncertainty about the next step all gave those conversations a purpose. I worked to communicate why attending could help students explore their options.
From outreach to attendance

I helped bring more than fifty students to the fair. The conversations turned into people physically showing up to explore opportunities, ask questions, and consider a path they might not have taken otherwise.

That was a tangible result for me. It connected the social skills I had developed at university with work that mattered to an organization. It also showed me that the responsibility continues after getting someone’s attention: they are trusting your recommendation with their time.
Working with the team

The role involved maintaining a positive, professional relationship with the Studypedia team as well as reaching students. My LinkedIn description reflects pride in that relationship and an ongoing connection to its educational mission.

The fair photographs capture both sides of the experience: representing the agency and being part of the team around the event. They are reminders of a period when I was discovering how naturally teaching, communication, and business could overlap.
What I carried forward
This experience helped me recognize the value of the relationships I was building. Outreach worked through conversations with people, shaped by an understanding of what they were looking for.
That remains relevant to my work in education today. An opportunity can exist on paper, but helping someone take the first step toward it takes attention, clear communication, and trust.
takeaway: Trust makes an invitation worth considering. Follow-through makes it meaningful.
images: At Studypedia’s second International Educational Fair, October 2022.
The team around the fair. Both photographs come from the LinkedIn project.

name: Docubid
title: When tutoring became a network.
deck: A role spanning student support, writing, and brand ambassadorship—and another step in learning how to work with people at scale.
sections: Demand beyond one person

Tutoring began as something I could do myself, then grew into a network of instructors. Eventually, demand and the changing availability of that team made it difficult to handle every request within the same setup. Docubid became one of the ways I could connect students with additional support.

I referred students to the platform and also tutored through it. On LinkedIn, I describe the role as Writer and Brand Ambassador: a combination of academic support, written content, client communication, and outreach.
Explaining the service

My ambassador work involved promoting Docubid’s services through personalized communication and community engagement. It built on the relationships I had developed as a tutor and the trust students placed in me when they asked where to find help.

My LinkedIn account records onboarding more than fifty clients within one month. The important part of that experience for me was the connection between communication and action: understanding a request, explaining the available support, and helping someone take a next step.
The work behind the referral

The role included writing and editing across academic subjects, alongside tutoring. Those responsibilities called on different aspects of communication: organizing ideas on a page, adapting an explanation, and responding to what a person was struggling to understand.

In tutoring, I worked to simplify complex material and approach a concept from more than one angle. That had already become central to how I learned myself. Explaining something clearly meant first recognizing where the difficulty was for the person in front of me.
A small piece of the outreach

The promotional card saved with this project on LinkedIn carries my KF20 code. It is a concrete piece of the ambassador work—a small artifact from a role that otherwise happened largely through conversations, referrals, and support.

It also captures the overlap I was beginning to understand between education and business. Helping people find a service involves communication and relationships; delivering the support requires care and follow-through. Both sides influence whether that relationship continues.
What the experience added

Docubid gave me further practice in client relations, written communication, and explaining services. It also showed me how a teaching network could connect with a wider organization when one person or one small team could not handle everything.
The experience sits within a longer thread in my work: learning something, making it understandable, and finding ways to connect people with the help they need.
takeaway: A network grows through relationships. Its value depends on what happens after the introduction.
images: The KF20 promotional card from my Docubid ambassador work.

name: FRÉA / L’Oréal Brandstorm
title: What could a different beauty routine look like?
deck: A university competition concept exploring convenience, inclusion, and sustainability within one product idea.
sections: An idea worth exploring

During my time at LAU, I worked with a team on FRÉA for L’Oréal Brandstorm. The proposal explored a makeup line designed around a different kind of routine: convenient to wear, considerate of different users, and more conscious of resource use and packaging.

For me, the project was an opportunity to turn broad ambitions into a concept that could be explained. Sustainability and inclusion are large ideas. A competition proposal asks you to connect them to specific product choices and show how those choices fit together.
The proposed product experience

At the center of FRÉA was a no-wash-off formula concept: makeup designed to break down overnight, with the aim of reducing the need for water and makeup remover. We also proposed skin-nourishing ingredients intended to replenish the skin during wear.

These were proposed product attributes in a competition concept, rather than a tested formulation or a launched range. The idea gave us a way to explore how convenience and environmental considerations could be discussed together in the same customer experience.
Inclusion and the surrounding choices

The proposal included a broad shade range intended to serve diverse users. It also specified recyclable packaging as part of the environmental direction. These choices widened the scope beyond the formula itself: who the product was for, how it was packaged, and how it could fit into a routine.

The concept was presented as adaptable across L’Oréal’s portfolio, spanning makeup brands such as L’Oréal Paris, Maybelline, and Urban Decay, and skincare brands such as Kiehl’s and La Roche-Posay. This was part of the team’s proposal, not a collaboration or adoption by those brands.
Learning to connect the pieces
The work combined a product idea with positioning and communication. The challenge was to make the different features read as one coherent concept, rather than a collection of desirable claims.

Looking back, I value the practice of connecting an ambitious idea to specific choices. The concept presentation preserved on LinkedIn captures that stage of learning: taking a question, giving it a shape, and making it understandable enough to discuss with others.
takeaway: An ambitious idea becomes easier to discuss when its choices are specific.
images: The FRÉA concept slide from the team presentation attached to my LinkedIn project.

name: Redseer / LAU Sailors Consulting
title: Making a case for a different kind of grocery business.
deck: A winning university case proposal for a UAE retailer, connecting Ramadan demand with technology, sustainability, and customer engagement.
role: LAU Sailors Consulting · Team case competition
sections: The business question

Our team, LAU Sailors Consulting, developed a growth strategy for Retail Co., an offline grocery chain in the UAE facing competitive challenges. The case asked us to think about how the business could regain momentum around Ramadan and build a stronger position over time.

Working as a team, we approached the problem through a combination of sustainability initiatives, technology proposals, marketing, and customer engagement. The presentation’s ambition was to help Retail Co. become a go-to e-grocery destination.
Connecting sustainability to participation

One part of the strategy proposed packaging-return programs linked to discounts, alongside a Green Vision campaign. The idea connected an environmental initiative with a reason for customers to participate and return.

It was useful to think about sustainability in the context of the customer relationship. A proposal needs to explain how the initiative fits into people’s behavior and the retailer’s offer, as well as what it aims to improve.
Technology and Ramadan engagement

Our technology proposals included augmented- and mixed-reality shopping experiences and UAE-themed NFTs aimed at younger consumers. Those ideas reflected the case’s 2022 context and were elements of the proposal, not deployed features.

The marketing plan included Ramadan-themed social filters, influencer collaborations, digital coupons, and personalized promotions. Iftar cooking classes and loyalty programs added ways for customers to engage with the brand beyond a single transaction. Together, the ideas explored several routes to a closer relationship with shoppers.
The forecast and the result

The proposal projected 14.5% revenue growth over 2022–2025. That figure was a forecast within our competition solution, rather than a measured commercial result. The practical outcome we can point to is the competition: our team won, as recorded in the certificate attached to my LinkedIn project.

The certificate is dated 3 February 2022 and names the Redseer Student Case Competition, “Unwrapping Ramadan 2022.” Alongside the deck cover, it preserves a specific moment from the work we did together.
What I took from the experience
This was practice in building an argument across several parts of a business. Research, commercial reasoning, customer understanding, and presentation all had to contribute to the same direction.

The experience helped me see strategy as something that needs to be explained and defended. An idea becomes more useful when other people can understand how it relates to the problem, what it asks the business to do, and what assumptions sit behind it.
takeaway: A strategy needs a clear argument connecting the customer, the business, and the proposed change.
images: The team’s RetailCo presentation cover, preserved from LinkedIn.
Winner’s certificate for “Unwrapping Ramadan 2022,” dated 3 February 2022.
